title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: when, where and how many

questions.prompt: A guide to earning degrees at a distance argues that this way of studying offers a flexibility a traditional programme cannot, since it leaves the learner free to work whenever and wherever he chooses. A pupil replies in a letter: you are mistaken, because an online course takes as much of a learner's time as a classroom course, if not more. Why does that reply fail to contradict the claim it is aimed at?

options.text: the reply agrees with the claim, flexibility and a heavy commitment being the same
the reply would contradict the claim only if the pupil had followed both kinds
the claim was about when and where the hours are spent; the reply is about how many there are
the claim was about how many hours are needed; the reply is about when and where they are spent

questions.explanation: Contradiction needs two statements about the same thing, and these two are not about the same thing. Freedom of hour and freedom of place say where in the week and where on the map the work happens; a time commitment says how much of the week it eats. A learner can have every hour of his own choosing and still owe the course as many hours as a classroom would have taken, so both statements can stand together untouched. Reversing which claim was about what leaves the same failure standing, only backwards. Calling the two the same thing is worse still: it would make a heavy course automatically a flexible one. And having followed both kinds of programme is not what this reply lacks — a reply that answered the claim would do its work whoever had written it.

questions.prompt: A page is going to press, and every line on it must show a phrase that explains the noun in front of it, fenced by a comma at each end. Tick EVERY line that is punctuated in that way.

options.text: Leila Ben Amor, the tutor of the evening course, answered every letter she was sent.
The review, a quarterly published in Tunis, printed three of the replies it received.
Sami Trabelsi, the youngest learner on the course gave up his television for a term.
The course an eight-month programme in three languages, opens in October.
The pupils wrote to the author, to the magazine and to their own teacher.

questions.explanation: Two lines are fenced at both ends and go to press as they stand: the phrase naming what Leila Ben Amor does sits between two commas immediately after her name, and the phrase saying what sort of publication the review is does the same job for it. In each case the explanation can be lifted out and a whole sentence remains. The line about Sami Trabelsi opens its fence and never closes it, so the reader is told an explanation has begun and left to guess where it stops; the line about the course does the opposite, closing a fence that was never opened, which is why the words run into each other in front of the comma. The line about the pupils is correctly punctuated and still fails the instruction: its commas are keeping the items of a list apart, which is the comma's other job on this page and not the one being checked.

questions.prompt: Three remarks printed under a lesson heading are said to come from learners writing to a magazine. A pupil treats all three as facts about online courses and quotes them in his own letter as proof that he is right. What is wrong with using them that way?

options.text: each is one learner's opinion, and quoting it proves little even about that learner
each was printed in a magazine, so quoting it without the magazine's leave is not allowed
each was made several years ago, so quoting it proves nothing that was not so at the time
each is one learner's opinion, so quoting it proves what was believed and not what is so

questions.explanation: A quotation is a witness, and a witness reports a belief. Put a learner's remark in your letter and you have established, quite solidly, that a learner held that view — which is worth having, and is not the same as establishing that the view is correct. The over-correction is just as bad: the remark is excellent evidence about its own author, and refusing it even that leaves you with nothing to argue from. Permission is a different question altogether and has nothing to do with whether an argument holds. And age would only matter if the claim were about a year rather than about how learning works; a remark from 2003 about the hours a course costs is answerable today on its merits.

questions.prompt: A learner says he cannot follow the course because he has no time. He is told that somebody short of time can make more of it. He answers that a day holds twenty-four hours and that nobody has ever added a twenty-fifth. What has he misunderstood?

options.text: making time means moving hours from one use to another, not adding hours to a day
making time means adding hours to a day, which is precisely what he has just denied
making time means asking for extra days, which is what he was in fact being offered
making time means counting the hours he already holds, which he has not yet done

questions.explanation: He is right about the day and wrong about the phrase. Nobody was proposing to lengthen anything: to make time is to find hours that are already committed and commit them elsewhere, which is exactly what the printed example does when it takes them out of sleep. Read the phrase as an addition of hours, as he has, and the objection becomes unanswerable — that is the sign that the reading is wrong, since the remark was made by somebody who also knew how long a day is. Extra days were never on offer, and a course with no fixed end would still have to be fitted into the weeks that exist. Counting would tell him the size of the problem and move not one hour of it.

questions.prompt: A pupil has granted, in his letter, that a distance learner may choose his own hour and his own place. He must now counter the claim without withdrawing what he has just granted, and without giving offence. Which sentence does that?

options.text: Anybody who thinks that freedom worth having has never sat down to a course.
The freedom is real, and it is the very thing that lets a week go by with nothing done.
The freedom is not real at all, since the course still has to be over by a fixed date.
The freedom is real enough, and I have nothing that I could put beside it.

questions.explanation: The strong move keeps the concession and turns it: the freedom stands, and the very thing that makes it valuable is shown to carry a cost with it. Nothing has been taken back and nobody has been insulted, yet the claim no longer stands alone. Denying that the freedom is real cancels the grant outright and reopens an argument the pupil had already settled in the other man's favour — the deadline limits when the work must end, not when it may be done. Granting the point and confessing there is nothing to set beside it is polite and is not a counter at all. And an insult counters a person instead of a claim, which is the one thing the instruction rules out.

questions.prompt: A learner writes one sentence about the hours an online course wants, and in the middle of it he fences three words with a comma at each end: like all learning. A classmate says those three words could simply be deleted, since the sentence works perfectly well without them. What would the sentence lose?

options.text: the claim that time is the only thing that any kind of learning has ever demanded
nothing whatever: the words repeat what the rest of the sentence has already said
the claim that this kind of learning is no exception to a demand every kind makes
the claim that this kind of learning demands rather more time than any other kind

questions.explanation: The classmate is right about the grammar and wrong about the sentence. Fence the three words out and what remains is a complete statement — that is what makes them an addition. But they were carrying the argument: by putting this kind of learning beside every other kind, they refuse it any special case, which is the answer to the reader who came to the page believing that a course followed at home is a lighter thing. They claim no extra burden, only an equal one, so reading them as a complaint about a heavier load says something the sentence never said. They say nothing about time being all that learning wants, either — attention, patience and a place to work go unmentioned rather than denied. And repetition is the one thing they are not: nothing else in the line mentions any other kind of learning at all.
